articles.title: 'Every day there is killing': Gazans face Israeli strikes despite ceasefire as peace deal stalls - BBC
articles.summary: 'Every day there is killing': Gazans face Israeli strikes despite ceasefire as peace deal stalls  BBCGaza ceasefire ‘exists in name only’, more than 100 NGOs say  Al Jazeera‘Neither war nor peace’: Palestinians in Gaza on existing amid disease, despair and ruins  The GuardianIsrael’s ‘scorched-earth’ ceasefire in Gaza  Financial TimesLife in Gaza still 'absolutely horrendous' - UN official  RTE.ie
articles.full_text:
In her tent in central Gaza early one morning last month, 31-year-old Fida al-Toutah, a mother of five, was combing her daughter's hair when the sound of gunfire erupted.
"My mother shouted at us to get down," her son Ezz recalled, weeping as he spoke.
He only realised Fida had been hit when he saw the bloodied hands of his younger brother, who had been clinging onto his mother as the bullets came in.
"Our mother was so kind and generous. What did she do wrong?" Ezz said.
Fida died on 21 September from a gunshot wound to the head.
She is among more than 1,400 people in Gaza who have been killed in Israeli attacks since the start of the ceasefire on 10 October last year, according to Gaza's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
The ceasefire saw thousands of Palestinians held by Israel released in return for all of the 48 remaining hostages held in Gaza, and an agreement to end the war - which was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 taken hostage.
On the ground in Gaza, it meant that Israel's large-scale bombardment stopped, which brought substantial relief and an increase in humanitarian aid and medical supplies entering the territory.
But even during the ceasefire, Israel has continued launching strikes in Gaza almost every day. In the past week alone more than 30 people have been killed, according to Gaza's health ministry.
Israel says it is targeting Hamas operatives, and accuses Hamas of continued violations of the ceasefire.
"It [the ceasefire] is all lies. Every day there's a shooting. Every day there is killing and death lurking around," said Ahed, Fida's husband.
In response to the BBC's questions about Fida's killing, the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said they had no record of the incident.
The total death toll from Israeli attacks since the start of the war in Gaza three years ago now stands at more than 74,000, according to the Gaza health ministry.
Outside Fida's tent, her brother Ibrahim pointed to the holes he said were made by a volley of bullets fired by Israeli forces.
"This tent is just a piece of cloth. Imagine that a military vehicle came down here and fired a spray of bullets," he said. "There was also gunfire coming from the sky, from above, from quadcopters, and it was directed at unarmed civilians."
Fida is the fourth of Ibrahim's siblings to be killed since the start of the war. "We left our neighbourhood Zeitoun to survive, but death is following us," he said.
The family has moved seven times but safety has been out of reach. Most of Gaza's 2.1 million population has been displaced multiple times by the war, the UN says, with many forced to live in tented cities and unsafe structures.
On the same day that Fida was killed, 14-year-old Ismail al-Bardawil was also shot dead. He was killed in the al-Mawasi area of Rafah, in southern Gaza.
His family told the BBC that he was shot by Israeli forces while he and his brothers were fishing in the Mediterranean Sea, around 20m (66ft) from the shore. He is one of more than 300 children killed since the start of the ceasefire, according to Gaza's health ministry.
The IDF said it had no information about this incident either.
Over the past year, the IDF has released videos of its operations in Gaza targeted at Hamas and other groups. At least seven Israeli soldiers have been killed in Gaza since the start of the ceasefire.
Both Fida and Ismail lived close to the so-called Yellow Line that separates the areas occupied by the Israeli military in Gaza from areas controlled by Hamas in the west.
Areas around the line are considered the most dangerous because Israeli forces have frequently opened fire there. But there are few options to move because there is an extreme shortage of space.
The strip was densely populated even before the war began. Now, its population is squeezed into under 40% of its area, which is controlled by Hamas.
In those areas the group maintains a tight grip, clamping down on dissent and still recruiting fighters.
In May this year, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said he had directed the IDF to increase the area of Gaza under Israel's control to 70%.
Architect Amal Alabadla, who lived in a comfortable flat prior to the war, now lives in a tent on the coastline.
"Every time the rains come, it gets flooded. I feel very scared when the wind is strong because our tent gets destroyed or damaged," she said.
Amal is forced to raise her two boys - Mohammed and Noah - on her own.
Her husband was not in Gaza when the war broke out, and in three years they have not been reunited. Amal's three brothers, who helped her care for the boys, were killed in separate attacks before the ceasefire began.
"During the winter, my son suffers from epilepsy seizures because of the cold. It's very hard sometimes to keep him dry and warm," she said.
"Before the war, I had a job, a house, an ordinary life, but then everything turned upside down. Now we have no hope, nothing. It's only about survival day by day, to keep my kids alive, clean, healthy and fed."
There are camps further inland in Gaza that have even been built below sea level, which are at greater risk of flooding.
The October 2025 peace deal was supposed to pave the way for the reconstruction in Gaza, but rebuilding has not yet begun - stuck in limbo because of an impasse over the second phase of the deal.
Israel strictly controls what materials and machinery are allowed into Gaza, acting, it says, for reasons of its own security.
Earlier this year, US President Donald Trump put forward a plan to disarm Hamas, but in August it was rejected by Netanyahu, who stated that no military pull-out would happen until Hamas was "genuinely" disarmed.
Hamas has said handing over its heavy weapons is contingent on Israel ending "all forms of aggression" and withdrawing its forces from Gaza.
Half a world away, Trump's Board of Peace has also proposed a recovery plan for Gaza worth $2.45bn (£1.85bn).
But, one year on from the ceasefire and three years on from the start of the war, many like Amal are deeply sceptical of things actually changing on the ground.
"We are struggling and not being allowed to rebuild," she said. "I don't think they are telling us the truth about allowing us to rebuild a safe future for our children."

articles.title: Trump Is Gutting America’s Core Geopolitical Advantage
articles.summary: Robert Zoellick, an expert on the global economy who served as U.S. trade representative and World Bank president, makes the authoritative case that President Donald Trump’s antagonism toward Canada and Mexico is destroying an economic and security partnership that that enables the United States to project power globally.
articles.full_text:
The Trump administration’s attack on Canada and Mexico is cracking the foundation of the United States’ global power. Friendly relations with neighbors enhance security, promote mutual economic gain, and make it easier to handle transnational challenges. Weak neighbors export trouble. Today, Canadians perceive U.S. President Donald Trump’s high tariffs and belittling of their country as the “51st state” as assaults on Canada’s economy and independence. In Mexico, Trump’s economic coercion and threats of military intervention have revived deep historical anxieties about gringo hegemony.
The North American partnership took generations to forge. During the nineteenth century, the United States’ foreign policy concentrated on its home continent, where it competed with France, Mexico, Russia, Spain, the United Kingdom, and indigenous peoples for dominance. As the United States became a global power in the twentieth century, U.S. strategists took North American relations for granted. Washington turned its attention to Europe, the Asia-Pacific, and the Middle East. Since the closing years of the Cold War, however, U.S. presidents have recognized the need to invest in North America. Ronald Reagan laid out the strategic rationale clearly when he launched his presidential campaign in 1979: “The key to our own future security may lie in both Canada and Mexico becoming much stronger than they are today,” he explained. “It is time we stopped treating our nearest neighbors as foreigners.”
Geopolitics begin with geography, and the United States’ geography gives it an enormous advantage over the world’s other major powers. China and Russia each have to manage relationships with 14 neighbors, many of which are unfriendly or carry resentments from histories of conflict. India must deal with six, including a nuclear-armed rival. All three powers’ access to the world’s seas depends on passage through maritime chokepoints. In contrast, the United States borders two benign neighbors and enjoys open sailing on two vast oceans. Close cooperation with Canada and Mexico enhances homeland security, attracts investment, promotes innovation, creates a huge market rich in resources and talent, and helps all three countries deal with criminal networks, illegal immigration, and threats to clean air, water, and wildlife.
A safe, resilient, and adaptive North America is the starting point of U.S. global strategy. Washington is best positioned to navigate an uncertain world when the United States, Canada, and Mexico present a common front. Yet Trump’s bullying is driving the United States’ natural partners away. The president is destroying a precious geopolitical asset: a strong continental base from which Washington projects power.
CONTINENTAL VISION
William Seward, who served as U.S. secretary of state from 1861 to 1869, first appreciated that good relations with the United States’ neighbors would boost the country’s global influence. He asserted that to have “control of this continent is to be . . . the controlling interest in the world.” When he was negotiating the U.S. purchase of Alaska in 1867, Seward observed that Alaska and the Aleutian Islands “extend[ed] a friendly hand to Asia.” He also tried to buy Greenland, Iceland, the Hawaiian Islands, and islands in the Caribbean, hoping that the purchases would help secure the United States’ oceanic approaches.
Seward recognized, however, that the United States could also boost its power by strengthening economic links, not just by adding territory. He abhorred European imperial conquests of foreign lands. He had also opposed the 1846–48 U.S. war with Mexico. At the end of the U.S. Civil War in 1865, Seward prevented Generals Ulysses S. Grant and Philip Sheridan from invading Mexico to depose the Habsburg archduke whom the French had installed as emperor. He reasoned that an invasion would arouse Mexican hostility and that the Mexicans could depose the interloper themselves—which they did, in 1867.
 The United States’ geography gives it an enormous advantage.
Seward dealt diplomatically with the United States’ northern neighbor, too. In 1867, the British government united its North American colonies to form the Canadian Confederation, in part to deter Washington from invading Canada in retaliation for London’s assistance to the Confederacy during the Civil War. Seward responded by choosing the peaceful path of arbitration to resolve wartime claims against the United Kingdom.
Seward envisioned a North American union created through free choice, not coercion or conquest. He believed in the attractive power of the United States. Commerce, he maintained, would be the new “god of boundaries” that would redraw borders and pull countries together. Ernest Paolino, his biographer, termed this idea Seward’s “law of imperial gravity.”
The restoration of Mexican President Benito Juarez in 1867, the same year the Canadian Confederation was formed, offered the prospect of a democratic North America with closer economic ties. The neighbors did establish peaceful relations. But Seward’s vision faded in later decades as Americans focused their sights westward, paying less attention to their neighbors to the north and south.
A SEARCH FOR STABILITY
By the early twentieth century, the United States had come to take continental harmony for granted. The Mexican Revolution of 1910 ended that sense of security. In the decade of violent conflicts that followed, attacks on border towns and seizures of American property by revolutionaries and bandits prompted the United States to send two military expeditions into Mexico. Washington narrowly avoided a quagmire. U.S. President Woodrow Wilson’s reelection campaign slogan in 1916, “He kept us out of war,” referred as much to Mexico as Europe. Still, the instability on its doorstep made the United States vulnerable. In 1917, imperial Germany sent the new Mexican government a secret proposal of alliance—a message intercepted by the British—that promised German assistance in recovering Arizona, New Mexico, and Texas if Mexico were to side with Germany in the event the United States entered World War I.
The United States was able to stabilize relations with the one-party authoritarian state that consolidated control in Mexico in the 1920s. As the political scientist Pamela Starr explained, Washington accepted its neighbor’s autonomy, but “within limits.” As long as Mexico did not threaten U.S. security, the United States would not interfere. Mexico’s stability was more important than challenging its stunted democracy, prickly nationalism, and closed economy. This arrangement lasted about 50 years, during which the two countries found ways to cooperate. Between 1942 and 1964, for instance, the United States’ Bracero Program offered some 4.6 million Mexicans guest worker permits, filling labor gaps in the agriculture, railroad, and other industries.
The twentieth century also saw Canada transition from British dominion to sovereign North American partner and ally. During the 1920s and 1930s, the United States and Canada built bridges and tunnels to boost economic exchanges. U.S. Secretary of State Cordell Hull negotiated important reciprocal trade agreements with Canada in 1935 and 1938. After World War II, Canadians fought beside Americans in the Korean War and vigorously supported the establishment of NATO, the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, the United Nations, and other institutions that made up the postwar order. During the 1950s, the United States and Canada constructed the St. Lawrence Seaway. The two countries also established a vast radar system to monitor possible missile attacks over the Arctic. In 1965, they signed a pact creating a duty-free integrated automobile market.
TIES THAT BIND
The pace of North American integration picked up during the Reagan administration. Reagan’s outreach to his Canadian counterpart, Prime Minister Brian Mulroney, encouraged Mulroney to propose an expansive free trade agreement in 1985. Mulroney ran a big risk: Canadians were wary of becoming economically dependent on or dominated by the United States, but they also wanted rules to discipline U.S. trade practices and encourage investment. The two countries concluded the agreement in 1987, and the U.S. Congress approved it the following year. The 1988 Canadian elections effectively became a referendum on the trade deal—one that Mulroney won.
Carlos Salinas, who assumed the Mexican presidency that year, recognized that a similar agreement would open up his country’s economy and attract investment. Mexico was struggling with debt crises, declining energy revenues, and the related breakdown of the ruling party’s half-century-old corporatist model, which had fostered a centralized, closed economy. Looking to escape stagnation and to spur reform, Salinas took the bold step of proposing a free trade agreement to President George H. W. Bush in 1990.

articles.title: Iran’s Theory of Victory
articles.summary: Tehran’s fight for great-power status in the post-American Middle East.
articles.full_text:
When it comes to Iran, the Trump administration has a decidedly dismal record. It failed to wear down the Islamic Republic with months of intense bombings. It could not bend Iran’s will at the negotiating table. Yet despite seven months of setbacks, U.S. officials believe that they have turned the page. They have implemented fresh sanctions while maintaining the existing American blockade of the country’s southern coast, throttling its access to outside commerce. As a result, they have concluded that the Islamic Republic will soon either concede or be downed. “We are going to economically asphyxiate this regime,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent declared on September 1.
There is no doubt that Washington has dealt significant damage to Iran. But the Islamic Republic does not believe it is unraveling. In fact, Tehran thinks that it will defeat the United States—and it isn’t hard to see why. The Iranian government did not merely survive the U.S.-Israeli bombardment. It retaliated ferociously, damaging American military bases and obstructing the Strait of Hormuz. Its people are paying a hefty economic price thanks to damage caused by the war and Washington’s cutoffs, but much of the population has rallied around the flag and seems to accept that hardship is necessary if Iran is to defend itself. As a result, Tehran has been emboldened. Its officials may not see eye to eye on each tactic. But they share the same ambitions: evicting U.S. forces from the Persian Gulf, forcing Washington to remove all its sanctions, and getting the United States to accept that Iran is a great power.
This agenda might sound overly audacious, given that Iran has been materially weakened. But the Islamic Republic thinks its aims are within reach. It believes its military can drive U.S. troops from the Persian Gulf by continuing to strike American bases directly and by getting Arab countries to push the United States to leave. It thinks that by wreaking havoc on energy markets, it can force Washington to lift economic restrictions, as well. Tehran’s theory of victory, in other words, is that it can hold out and inflict enough pain that the United States will end its containment of Iran.
CLOSING RANKS
No one doubts that Iran has been battered by war. Months of American and Israeli bombs have damaged the country’s industries and infrastructure, spiking unemployment and pushing more Iranians into poverty. Washington’s sanctions and naval blockade have caused rampant inflation. And the American and Israeli militaries can count many tactical successes, including the assassination of former Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei.
But strategically, the conflict has been disastrous. U.S. officials believed that punishing aerial bombardments and sweeping efforts to degrade the Iranian economy would bring the Islamic Republic to its knees. They didn’t. Washington hoped that assassinating Khamenei would prompt a mass antigovernment uprising. That scheme also failed. Instead, Khamenei’s death brought out the Islamic Republic’s ardent supporters. They marched every night in the country’s main cities and were eventually joined by Iranians of other political hues, who rallied in support of their homeland. When the war started, Turkey planned to accommodate 70,000 Iranian refugees. But few people fled. In fact, as the war progressed, many Iranians living abroad returned home, including long-exiled cultural figures, journalists, and politicians, such as the singers Mohsen Namjoo and Bijan Mortazavi.
This surge in nationalism is not an endorsement of the Islamic Republic. Many Iranians remain deeply unhappy with the country’s leadership. But the anger at their government has been subsumed by their anger at Washington. Previously, most Iranians were skeptical of the Islamic Republic’s claim that the United States was bent on their country’s destruction and in fact hoped Tehran would seek better relations with Washington. But the bombings of Iranian cities and U.S. President Donald Trump’s repeated threats to annihilate the country’s civilization (saying, for example, that he might “blow the entire nation up” and drive it “into hell with no chance of survival”) have changed attitudes. Iranians across the political spectrum now do think that the United States wants to obliterate their country—or at least make it capitulate to every American demand.
 Iranians do not see the U.S.-Israeli war as liberating.
This conclusion was apparent in our lengthy conversations with Iranians of all ideologies, which we started conducting when Washington first bombed Iran, in June 2025, and have continued to the present, tracing their political attitudes over that period. The vast majority expressed deep distress and anger at their government after the massacres that took place in response to January’s mass protests. But we found that political opinions have shifted drastically as the war has dragged on and as Trump has upped his annihilatory rhetoric. “We believed so much in the American promise,” Ali, a 45-year-old long-time dissident who has spent years in prison for his activism on social and political issues, told us. “Yet with this war and everything that Trump and his administration have said and done, it’s obvious the Americans sold us a false bill of goods. They want nothing but Iran’s total submission, and that’s not acceptable to us.” Mahsa, a writer and artist in her 30s, relayed similar sentiments. “Everything we believed the [United States] stood for, freedom and respect and democracy, I now see as lies,” she said. “As angry as I’ve been at our state over the years, this is our homeland, and no outside country has the right to kill our leaders and drop bombs on our children and attempt to destroy us.”
Little wonder, then, that Khamenei’s July funeral procession drew millions of mourners, even though the country was in the midst of conflict. At the event, people handed out red flags, symbolizing their desire for bloody vengeance. Shortly after, Iran attacked commercial vessels crossing the Strait of Hormuz, unraveling the precarious cease-fire the country had struck with the United States three months earlier.
Many U.S. officials seem to think that stiff economic pressure will ultimately prompt a shift in opinion—that if they suffer enough, Iranians will decide to try overthrowing their government or that the Islamic Republic, fearing for its survival, will submit to American demands. But this is magical thinking. Iran has spent the past 15 years developing an economy specifically designed to withstand American economic warfare. Iranian officials, for instance, have forged strong relations with neighboring traders and made the country nearly self-sufficient when it comes to food. As a result, even though Iran’s economy is hurting and inflation is high, cities and towns have had no shortages of important goods or services to date. “It’s incredible how well-run everything has been inside of the country,” Hamid Reza, an engineer who regularly travels between Isfahan and Tehran for work, said. “Things are expensive, but there have been no shortages whatsoever across the country. Everything has been managed internally with a lot of care.”
That is not to say that Iranians feel optimistic about their country. They are anxious about the future, and they yearn for a return to calm and economic relief. But they do not see the U.S.-Israeli war as liberating. Instead, they see it as gratuitous aggression, and the resulting nationalism has blurred the lines between political factions and diminished the likelihood of another political uprising. The war, then, has strengthened the Islamic Republic.
PAIN AND GAIN
Much like its population, the Iranian government has adopted a more hostile view of Washington since the conflict began. The country’s new supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, has moved trusted lieutenants to key roles (even as he himself remains in hiding), and they are largely hard-line figures tied to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. These people, including Mohsen Rezaei, the national security adviser, and Hossein Taeb, the commander of Iran’s main domestic paramilitary forces, think deterring further attacks requires a decisive, aggressive response to any provocations. They are skeptical that Washington is serious about diplomacy. They point out that the United States has twice attacked Iran amid negotiations and then walked away from the memorandum of understanding it signed with Iran in June—and thus argue that it cannot be trusted. In fact, they believe that if the United States shows interest in talks, it might even be planning for renewed attacks, as it was in June 2025 and February 2026.
Iran’s relative moderates feel somewhat differently.
These elites, which include Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, Speaker of Parliament Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, former President Hasan Rouhani, and former Foreign Minister Mohammad Javad Zarif, have consistently argued that Tehran should keep looking for a diplomatic solution to the conflict.
Pezeshkian and Ghalibaf have highlighted the economic hardships facing ordinary people.
But the distance between them and the country’s hard-line leaders is not as great as it might seem.
As one analyst familiar with these figures told us, “No one is saying Iran should surrender.
” They may see economic relief as a top priority, yet their solution is to force the United States to implement the memorandum of understanding it signed in June.
That deal, in Iran’s view, committed Washington to unfreezing all of Iran’s assets, lifting all sanctions, never striking the country again, and paying reparations in exchange for nothing more than a cease-fire and renewed commerce through the Strait of Hormuz (on which Iran could still charge fees).
